content: Stretch marks, also known as striae in dermatology, are a type of scarring on the skin that often appear with a silvery-white hue. These marks result from tearing of the dermis, the middle layer of the skin, and while they may fade over time, they do not completely disappear. Stretch marks are commonly associated with pregnancy, obesity, rapid muscle growth (such as during bodybuilding), and the use of anabolic steroids. Although the skin is naturally elastic, rapid stretching can lead to permanent stretch marks. In medical terminology, stretch marks are referred to by various names depending on their cause or appearance, including striae distensae, striae atrophicae, lineae albicantes, and striae gravidarum (when caused by pregnancy). These marks occur when the skin's supportive structures, such as collagen and elastin fibers, are compromised. Glucocorticoid hormones, for example, can inhibit fibroblasts from producing these essential fibers, leading to a lack of structural support as the skin stretches. This results in tearing of both the dermis and epidermis. If the damage penetrates these layers, treatments like laser therapy cannot fully remove the marks. Certain medications, such as prednisolone, betamethasone dipropionate, and betamethasone valerate, are also known to cause stretch marks. Stretch marks initially appear as reddish or purplish lines but gradually fade to a lighter color. The affected areas often feel soft and appear empty. Human skin consists of three layers: the epidermis (outer layer), the dermis (middle layer), and the subcutaneous stratum (innermost layer). Stretch marks form in the dermis, which is responsible for maintaining the skin's shape and resilience. As long as the dermis remains supported, stretch marks will not form. However, stretching influences the location and direction of the marks, though it is not the sole cause. Stretch marks can develop anywhere on the body but are most commonly found in areas where fat is stored, such as the abdomen (especially near the belly button), breasts, upper arms, underarms, thighs (both inner and outer), hips, and buttocks. While they do not pose any health risks or impair the body's ability to function or repair itself, they are often a cosmetic concern. During pregnancy, between 75% and 90% of women develop stretch marks to some degree, typically appearing in the sixth or seventh month due to sustained hormonal changes. A randomized controlled study has shown that daily application of Gotu Kola extract, vitamin E, and collagen hydrolysates can significantly reduce the likelihood of developing stretch marks in susceptible women. However, while cocoa butter is an effective moisturizer, no research has demonstrated its ability to prevent or improve stretch marks. Various treatments aim to improve the appearance of existing stretch marks, including laser therapy, dermabrasion, and prescription retinoids. These treatments, when used daily for a month, have shown significant improvements in the length, depth, and irregular surface area of stretch marks. Some manufacturers claim that the best results are achieved on recent stretch marks, but there is limited evidence to support these claims. A surgical procedure known as a tummy tuck can remove lower abdominal stretch marks by excising the skin below the navel, where these marks frequently occur. Fractional laser resurfacing is a newer treatment modality that uses scattered pulses of light to target only a fraction of the scar tissue during each session. This creates microscopic wounds, stimulating the body to produce new collagen and epithelial tissue. This no downtime procedure has shown promising results, with clinical trials in 2007 reporting up to a 75% improvement in the appearance of stretch marks after 5–6 treatments. However, repeated pulsed dye laser treatments may increase pigmentation in individuals with darker skin tones.
